````text
This page doesn't cover most of what you asked for. It defers installation and configuration to other pages, so I can answer only part of the question from its content.

**Install command:** Not given. The page says to complete the installation steps first and links to the Installation page.

**Environment variables:**
- `LLM_API_KEY` is the only variable named. The Python example needs it; the CLI demo does not.
- `TELEMETRY_DISABLED=true` turns off anonymous telemetry. The page links to the setup-configuration overview for this.
- `LLM_PROVIDER`, `LLM_MODEL`, `EMBEDDING_PROVIDER`, `EMBEDDING_MODEL`, and `EMBEDDING_DIMENSIONS` are not mentioned.

**Minimal Python code:**

```python
import asyncio
import cognee

async def main():
    await cognee.forget(everything=True)           # wipes existing data and system state
    await cognee.remember("Cognee turns documents into AI memory.")
    results = await cognee.recall(query_text="What does Cognee do?")
    for result in results:
        print(result.text)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

**Storage backends:** The page doesn't name any default storage backends.

**Anthropic support:** Not mentioned.

**Gotchas:**
- **Async:** Most Cognee functions are `async` and must be awaited, so wrap calls in an `async` function and run it with `asyncio.run`.
- **Destructive reset:** `cognee.forget(everything=True)` clears all data and system state. The example calls it first to start clean, so remove it if you want to keep existing memory.
- **Model-dependent output:** Answer wording varies by provider and model.
- **`remember` does more than store:** It runs ingestion, chunking, entity extraction, graph building, and an enrichment pass, so it isn't instant.
- **First-run time:** Not stated.
- **Demo without a key:** `cognee-cli demo` runs offline with no LLM or embedding calls, then `cognee-cli forget --dataset demo` cleans up.

For installation and configuration details, see the Installation page (docs.cognee.ai/getting-started/installation) and the setup-configuration overview.
````

```text
**LLM variables**
- `LLM_PROVIDER`: default `openai`. Options include `openai`, `azure`, `gemini`, `anthropic`, `ollama`, `mistral`, `bedrock`, `llama_cpp`, and `custom`. If unset, it is inferred from the `LLM_MODEL` prefix.
- `LLM_MODEL`: default `openai/gpt-5.6-luna`, in `provider/model-name` format.
- `LLM_API_KEY`, `LLM_ENDPOINT`, `LLM_API_VERSION`: credentials and endpoint settings.

**Embedding variables**
- `EMBEDDING_PROVIDER`: default `openai`. Options include `openai`, `ollama`, `fastembed`, `gemini`, `mistral`, `bedrock`, `openai_compatible`, and `custom`. Note that Anthropic is not in this list.
- `EMBEDDING_MODEL`: default `openai/text-embedding-3-large`.
- `EMBEDDING_DIMENSIONS`: auto-derived, with a `3072` fallback. Set it explicitly for non-default models.
- `EMBEDDING_API_KEY`: falls back to `LLM_API_KEY` if unset.
- `EMBEDDING_ENDPOINT`: custom endpoint, required for some providers such as Ollama.

**Anthropic and embeddings**
Anthropic is available as an LLM provider but not as an embedding provider. If you set only the LLM to a non-OpenAI provider and leave the embedding settings at their defaults, Cognee raises `ProviderConfigMismatchError` at `add()` or `remember()`. To fix this, set `EMBEDDING_PROVIDER`, `EMBEDDING_MODEL`, and `EMBEDDING_API_KEY` for a supported embedding provider.

**Default databases** (all stored under `SYSTEM_ROOT_DIRECTORY/databases`)
- Relational: SQLite (`DB_PROVIDER=sqlite`)
- Vector: LanceDB (`VECTOR_DB_PROVIDER=lancedb`)
- Graph: Ladybug (`GRAPH_DATABASE_PROVIDER=ladybug`)

With no usable LLM key and no embedding settings, embeddings fall back to the local fastembed model `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`.
```

I found solid material on three of the six judges: Jan, Akash and, less certainly, Ankit. Fionn, David and Dominic have almost no public footprint. Searches on X, GitHub, news and gov.uk turned up nothing under those exact spellings, so for them I've given the organisation's context, marked as such. The event page lists judges by organisation only. https://luma.com/3k1pazop

## 1. Jan Stehlik, Briefcase (co-organiser)
- **Role:** Co-founder (listed as CTO) of Briefcase, which came out of Entrepreneur First in 2024. Reuben Steenkamp is CEO. https://www.joinef.com/?p=8981
- **Background:** Built and led product teams at Gousto, DAZN and Snyk. At the fintech Nous he was early in using LLMs to extract data from invoices, which is the core of Briefcase. https://finder.techleap.nl/news/feed/briefcase-secures-2-8m-for-ai-platform
- **What he's building:** A double-entry ledger built around AI, launched around 5 Oct 2026. "Autopilot" learns from every correction and posts items that pass its checks; unusual ones wait for review. The audit trail records every change, who made it and when. Customers report 97–99% accuracy. https://briefcase.so
- **Impress:** An agent that posts to a real ledger under explicit rules, sends exceptions to a human and leaves a clean audit trail.
- **Turn-off:** A chatbot bolted onto accounting, or confident numbers with no check that they reconcile.

## 2. Fionn O Colmain, Stripe (co-organiser)
- I found nothing public about Fionn beyond the event listing.
- **Stripe context:** Stripe's Agentic Commerce Suite, Shared Payment Tokens (which let an agent pass a buyer's payment details to a merchant) and the open Agentic Commerce Protocol. https://stripe.com/gb/newsroom/news/agentic-commerce-suite
- **Impress:** Real Stripe test-mode flows with spending limits, idempotency (retries can't pay twice), webhooks and refunds handled properly.
- **Turn-off:** Mocked payments, or an agent with unlimited power over the Stripe secret key.

## 3. David Gelberg, 10 Downing Street AI Team
- I found nothing public about David under this spelling.
- **Context:** The UK government's AI incubator, i.AI, builds open-source tools for civil servants (Humphrey, Consult, Redbox) and is now part of the Government Digital Service. https://github.com/i-dot-ai, https://civictech.guide/projects/incubator-for-artificial-intelligence-iai
- **Impress:** Accountability you can explain in public: a human sign-off, a readable log of decisions and protection for vulnerable users.
- **Turn-off:** "Fully autonomous, no human needed" when public or consumer money is involved.

## 4. Dominic Hudson, AI at Meta
- I found nothing public about Dominic.
- **Context (my guess, unverified):** Meta paid $1M for a Turing Institute fellowship that places AI engineers in i.AI to build tools on open models like Llama. That may be the link to judge 3. https://about.fb.com/news/2025/07/meta-backs-1-million-initiative-to-get-uks-best-ai-talent-to-build-tech-for-public-services/
- **Impress:** A sound design that can run on open models, with clear guardrails.
- **Turn-off:** A thin wrapper around a closed model's API.

## 5. Akash Bajwa, Earlybird (VC)
- **Key point:** Earlybird led Briefcase's seed round, so Akash is effectively a Briefcase investor. https://finder.techleap.nl/news/feed/briefcase-secures-2-8m-for-ai-platform
- **Writing:** Substack "Software Synthesis" (akashbajwa.co). None of his last 12 posts is about fintech or payments; he's more focused on agent infrastructure and strategy. https://www.akashbajwa.co/archive
  - "Agent Traffic" (14 Sep): over half of Cloudflare's traffic is non-human. Every request now needs an on-the-spot decision on whether the agent is authorised and whether to throttle, charge or block it. Agent identity could become a major security category. https://www.akashbajwa.co/p/agent-traffic-infrastructure-and
  - "Long-Horizon Agents" (2 Sep): background agents that run for a long time change computing and memory needs. https://www.akashbajwa.co/p/long-horizon-agents-compute-memory
  - "AI's Optimisation Era" (29 Jun): the moat is private evals tied to business outcomes, domain judgement and routing across cheaper models, not raw frontier capability. https://www.akashbajwa.co/p/ais-optimisation-era
- **Impress:** Agent identity and authorisation as a first-class design element, a private eval set with measured accuracy, and a credible path from hack to business.
- **Turn-off:** No moat (a GPT wrapper), or no numbers.

## 6. Ankit Jain, Google DeepMind
- **Likely match (self-published, unverified; the name is common):** Senior software engineer at DeepMind in London. He builds internal agentic tooling and multi-agent orchestration on Google's agent-to-agent (A2A) protocol. Previously at Microsoft, where he scaled M365 Copilot features and built LLM agents that cut Responsible AI evaluation time from 3 weeks to 2 days. https://hackernoon.com/u/loney7
- **Impress:** A clean multi-agent design (for example a separate policy or checker agent) and an automated evaluation of agent behaviour.
- **Turn-off:** A jumble of agents with no evals or tracing to show they work.

## What to aim for
Four judges point the same way: Jan (rules plus audit trail), Akash (identity, authorisation, evals), Ankit (multi-agent plus evals) and David (accountability). Pitch an agent that moves money through Stripe within an explicit policy. Each decision would be written to the Briefcase ledger with its reasoning, exceptions would go to a human, and you'd show a small eval proving the policy holds. Cognee memory could store learned rules and corrections, which matches Briefcase's "learns from every correction".

```text
**Products and launches**
- Allowance, a Y Combinator company, issues one-time virtual cards to agents with approval controls and limits. Users can approve or deny purchases in real time, and the agent never sees the user's real card number. Allowance gives AI agents one-time virtual cards with approval controls and built-in limits, so the agent never receives the user's actual card details.
- Oobit's Agent Cards give each agent its own card, with spend limits and merchant-category rules enforced at the transaction layer. Each agent gets its own programmable card, and finance teams can set spend limits, merchant category restrictions, and hard caps that have no override path.
- Corpay's Agent Card, launched July 2026, builds spending controls into AI-initiated transactions. It embeds spending controls directly into AI-initiated transactions to make autonomous procurement auditable.
- Cardia, a small private-beta product, gives each agent a card with per-merchant scope and a real-time authorizer that approves or denies each charge. A prompt-injected or hallucinating agent cannot spend outside the limits you set.

**Market context**
- Card networks and fintechs have expanded agent card programs. One guide says Visa, Mastercard, Amex, and Stripe all launched their own agent card programs between 2025 and 2026, each with different rules on reusability, approval flow, and fees.
- Adoption is still limited. Most purchases still require human approval as of mid-2026. Liability is unsettled: liability, security, and fee structures remain unresolved across the industry.
- Ramp notes that network-level standards like Visa Intelligent Commerce are now live.

**Design pattern**
Across sources, the common approach is a scoped card per agent or task, with limits checked at authorization time and revocation available. A developer-oriented piece argues that daily limit, monthly limit, and per-transaction cap should all be enforced at authorization time.
```

## Stripe for AI agents moving money: rundown as of 15 Oct 2026

### 1. Agent Toolkit and MCP
- **MCP server** at `https://mcp.stripe.com` (https://docs.stripe.com/mcp). It authenticates with OAuth, which can be scoped to sandboxes, or with an **agent API key** as a Bearer token. Setup is `claude mcp add --transport http stripe https://mcp.stripe.com/` or `stripe agent setup`. From December, full-access `sk_` keys and restricted keys without the Agent tag stop working; migrate by 30 Nov 2026.
- **Tools:** `stripe_api_search`, `stripe_api_details`, `stripe_api_read` (any GET), `stripe_api_write` (POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE on an allowlist: customers, refunds, PaymentIntents, invoices, subscriptions, payment links, disputes, Issuing reads, v2 money-management reads), `get_stripe_account_info`, `stripe_analytics`, and docs search. There are also **Treasury tools in public preview**: `get_balance_summary`, `send_money`, `setup_recipient`, `transfer_money`, `convert_currency`.
- Built-in **human confirmation**: a refund or outbound payment through `stripe_api_write` returns an approval URL that expires after 24h. You can see tool-call logs in Workbench.
- **Agent Toolkit repo** (https://github.com/stripe/agent-toolkit): the README now centres on MCP, agent skills/plugins, `@stripe/ai-sdk` (Vercel) and `@stripe/token-meter` (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini billing). It doesn't mention the older OpenAI Agents SDK, LangChain or CrewAI adapters. I didn't check npm or PyPI, so don't assume they're still maintained.

### 2. Issuing for agents
- https://docs.stripe.com/issuing/agents. Getting live access means applying in the Dashboard. Supported capabilities: per-agent virtual cards, single-use cards, `spending_controls[allowed_categories]` / `blocked_categories`, and `spending_limits[]` with `interval` set to `per_authorization` or `monthly`.
- **Real-time authorization:** Stripe sends an `issuing_authorization.request` webhook with card `metadata` (for example `agent_id` or `order_id`). You have a **2s timeout**, after which the card's default rules apply. Follow-up events: `issuing_authorization.created`, `issuing_transaction.created`, `issuing_dispute.updated`.
- **Merchant-ID locks are private preview.** Stick to MCC categories.
- **UK:** GB is one of 22 local-issuing countries (https://docs.stripe.com/issuing/global). The testing guide (https://docs.stripe.com/issuing/testing.md?testing-method=with-code) covers UK sandbox funding through **funding instructions (push)**, not US-style top-ups. Simulate purchases with `POST /v1/test_helpers/issuing/authorizations`, then `.../{id}/capture`.
- **Gotchas:**
  - I couldn't confirm that a fresh GB sandbox has Issuing enabled without applying. Check Dashboard → Issuing in the sandbox first.
  - Register the auth endpoint in Issuing settings.
  - Use a GB cardholder address and `currency=gbp`.
  - Keep any LLM call out of the 2s path.

### 3. Agentic commerce
- **ACP** was co-developed with OpenAI and powers ChatGPT Instant Checkout (https://stripe.com/newsroom/news/stripe-openai-instant-checkout).
- **Shared Payment Tokens** (https://docs.stripe.com/agentic-commerce/concepts/shared-payment-tokens.md?agent-seller=agent):
  - Call: `POST /v1/shared_payment/issued_tokens` with `usage_limits[max_amount|currency|expires_at]` and `seller_details[network_business_profile]`, plus `/revoke`.
  - Header: `Stripe-Version: 2026-09-30.preview`.
  - Test seller profile: `profile_test_61TU90nIeGjU7NNVXA6TU90m7ISQWsBxpcx9lASWWXTk`.
  - **GB is supported.** It is a preview with its own agentic-commerce terms of service, and the testing page is private preview.
- **MPP (Machine Payments Protocol, Stripe + Tempo)** (https://docs.stripe.com/payments/machine/mpp.md): HTTP 402 pay-per-call. It works in a **sandbox**: `npx mppx validate` runs test round-trips and Tempo testnet is configured automatically. x402 on Base is also supported. **Stablecoin acceptance is for US businesses only (not NY)**; everyone else has to email for access.
- **Onelink agent wallet / link-cli** (https://link.com/agents): **US only**, waitlist elsewhere.
- **Order Intents:** private preview, and its docs page now returns 404.
- **Stablecoin-backed Issuing cards:** private preview.

### 4. Money-out primitives
- **Fully usable in a GB sandbox:** Refunds, Disputes, Invoicing, PaymentIntents, Payouts, Connect transfers.
- **Treasury / v2 Financial Accounts** (https://docs.stripe.com/treasury): **UK is public preview**, but creating accounts and adding currencies happens in the Dashboard.
- **Global Payouts** (https://docs.stripe.com/global-payouts): **available to GB and US**, requires Treasury, and is aimed at businesses holding an MTL. Probably too much setup for tonight.

### 5. Stripe's own "policy" and "audit" tools
- **Agent-tagged restricted keys** (https://docs.stripe.com/keys.md#agent-keys) are automatically subject to **approval rules** (https://docs.stripe.com/account/approvals.md):
  - Conditions can be based on amount, actor, or rate.
  - The action is either "Require approval" or "Block".
  - When approval is needed the API returns an `approval_required` error.
  - Webhooks: `v2.core.approval_request.*`.
  - Everything is logged in Security history and Workbench.
- Built-in default rules for agent-tagged keys cover refunds and subscription cancellations. The keys page also mentions payouts, but the approvals page's list of supported actions doesn't, so treat payouts as unconfirmed.
- On single-member accounts, two-party rules only work with the agent-key actor condition.
- The Sessions 2026 developer keynote talks about "deterministic tools so agent actions are predictable and auditable" (https://stripe.com/sessions/2026/developer-keynote).
- **Fionn O Colmain:** I found no public profile, talks or posts. The event page (https://luma.com/3k1pazop) lists him as a Stripe judge and co-organiser with Jan Stehlik of Briefcase. His role isn't stated, so ask him in person. The page lists two tracks, revealed at the briefing, and Stripe credit prizes of £5k, £3k and £1k.

### Best primitives for a 3-hour demo of an agent moving money under policy

**1. Issuing virtual card per agent task, with real-time auth as the policy engine.** This is the strongest fit for "autonomy, policy, auditability".
- Each task gets a card with `spending_controls` and `metadata`.
- Your webhook checks a written policy (budget, MCC, velocity) and approves or declines in under 2s.
- Log each decision and its reason to Briefcase (ledger) and Cognee (memory).
- Drive purchases with the test helpers.
- *Gotchas:* Issuing being enabled in the GB sandbox is unverified, so check it in the first 10 minutes. The 2s timeout means deterministic rules in the hot path. Use UK push funding.

**2. Agent-tagged restricted key plus approval rules, for refunds, invoices and PaymentIntents.**
- Example: the agent issues refunds, anything over £50 returns `approval_required`, a human approves, and a webhook resumes the flow.
- You get a Stripe-native human-in-the-loop and audit trail with almost no code. It pairs well with the MCP server.
- *Gotchas:* uses the v2 preview API version. Sandbox support for approval rules wasn't confirmed. The supported-action list is narrow, with no transfers listed.

**3. SPT or MPP for agent-to-seller payments.**
- The agent mints a token capped by `max_amount` and `expires_at`, can revoke it, and pays a 402-gated API.
- *Gotchas:* preview terms. link-cli is US only, so build your own Payment Element plus the SPT issue call. Stablecoins are US only.

Fallback if Issuing isn't enabled: build #2 plus a policy layer you write yourself around Refunds and Invoices.

# Sponsor dossier: Briefcase and Cognee (London, 15 Oct 2026)

**Event:** "Stripe x Briefcase: AI FinTech London Hackathon" ([luma](https://luma.com/3k1pazop)). Hacking runs 6:00 to 9:00 PM and code freezes at 9:00. There are two tracks, which are announced at the 5:45 briefing. Prizes are £2k for the overall winner and £5k/£3k/£1k in Stripe credits for track winners. Judges are Jan Stehlik (Briefcase), Fionn O Colmain (Stripe), David Gelberg (No.10 AI team), Dominic Hudson (Meta), Akash Bajwa (Earlybird, Briefcase's lead investor) and Ankit Jain (DeepMind). The listing doesn't mention a Briefcase sandbox or Cognee credits.

---

## Briefcase

**What it is.** AI bookkeeping for UK businesses. It captures receipts and invoices (WhatsApp, email, upload), reconciles them against bank lines, handles prepayments and accruals, runs the month-end close, and files VAT/MTD returns to HMRC. It has two products:
- **Briefcase Ledger** is its own double-entry general ledger, launched 5 Oct 2026.
- **Briefcase Connect** adds the automation on top of Xero or QuickBooks.

Its main customers are accounting firms (Connolly, Wilson Partners, Price Bailey, Kreston Reeves and others). It claims 200 firms serving 6,000+ businesses. Pricing is £19, £39, £79 or £119 a month depending on volume, with a 14-day trial. It already has a native Stripe feed that reconciles payments, fees and payouts. Supplier payments go over open banking, gated by approval policies set by amount and approver. Company facts: founded at Entrepreneurs First in 2024, about $3M seed led by Earlybird, CEO Reuben Steenkamp, CTO Jan Stehlik. ([home](https://briefcase.so), [pricing](https://briefcase.so/pricing), [Ledger launch](https://briefcase.so/blog/uks-first-general-ledger-built-for-ai.md), [TFN](https://techfundingnews.com/ex-starling-bank-executives-briefcase-snaps-3m-to-transform-accounting-with-ai-automation/))

**Dev surface.** There is no public REST API or SDK; MCP is the only way in.
- **MCP server:** `https://api.briefcase.so/mcp`. You sign in through the browser and pick which businesses the assistant can see. It acts with your own permissions.
- **Claude Code:** `/plugin marketplace add Briefcase-AI/briefcase-plugin`, then `/plugin install briefcase@briefcase`, then sign in via `/mcp`. Other MCP clients can add the URL as a custom connector.
- **50 tools (31 read, 19 write):**
  - Transactions: list, get, update, publish, archive.
  - Bank statements and bank transactions.
  - Month-end close items and the close tracker.
  - Expense claims.
  - Ledger only: P&L, balance sheet, aged reports, create manual journal, raise sales invoice.
  - "List AI memories".
- **Safety limits:** Publishing, posting journals and raising invoices show a preview and need confirmation. The MCP cannot make payments or transfer funds.

([MCP page](https://briefcase.so/mcp), [connect guide](https://briefcase.so/articles/how-do-i-connect-claude-or-chatgpt-to-briefcase.md))

**What they'd likely want built** (my inference from their content):
- **Verification over review.** Jan's thesis is that agents should be checked automatically, not approved by a human. The demo would be an agent whose money moves are checked by deterministic rules, with every decision explained. ([blog, Mar 2026](https://briefcase.so/blog/build-for-verification-not-review.md))
- **Autopilot-style gating.** Their Autopilot only posts an invoice if it passes three checks: re-extraction agrees, the data is complete, and history is consistent (a Bayesian score above about 0.8). Otherwise it flags the item. Corrections lower future confidence and approvals raise it. ([Building autopilot](https://briefcase.so/blog/building-autopilot.md))
- **The gap the event points at.** Briefcase's MCP deliberately can't move money, and Stripe can. A strong build: an agent pays or refunds via Stripe (test mode) under a policy (limits, approvers), then reconciles and journals the move in Briefcase. It should leave an audit trail and feed the month-end close.
- **Memory.** They already have per-client "contextual learning" (similar past invoices retrieved per client) and "AI memories", which learn a business's conventions (17 Aug changelog). ([contextual learning](https://briefcase.so/blog/introducing-contextual-learning-in-the-world-of-ai-accounting.md), [changelog](https://briefcase.so/changelog.md))

**Risks and gotchas:**
- MCP access has to be switched on per workspace by Briefcase, and it's unclear whether trial accounts get it. Ask Jan or the team at the start for a demo workspace.
- Ledger-only tools (journals, P&L, invoicing, bank transactions) need a Ledger workspace, not a Connect one.
- It's UK-specific (VAT, MTD, HMRC), so use GBP and UK VAT in demo data.
- Without access, you'll need to mock the ledger. Mirror their MCP tool names so the demo still reads as native.

---

## Cognee

**What it is.** An open-source memory layer for agents (Apache-licensed Python). It combines a knowledge graph, vector search and a relational store. The latest release is v1.6.1 (24 Sep 2026); one breaking change in it makes `dlt` a core dependency. ([GitHub](https://github.com/topoteretes/cognee))

**Dev surface** (realistically 15–30 minutes to get running):
- `pip install cognee`, then set `LLM_API_KEY` (defaults to OpenAI for both the LLM and embeddings).
- The v1 API is async:

```python
await cognee.remember(text, dataset_name="policies")
res = await cognee.recall(query_text="Is this payee approved?", datasets=["policies"])
```

- `improve` enriches the graph and moves session memory into the permanent graph. `forget` deletes data.
- The older `add` / `cognify` / `search(search_type=GRAPH_COMPLETION)` / `memify` calls are documented as "still available".
- Default stores are local, so nothing else to install: SQLite, LanceDB, and a Ladybug graph store.
- **MCP:** `cognee-mcp` runs via `docker compose --profile mcp` on port 8001.
- **Cloud:** 14-day free trial, sign in with Google or GitHub. Requests go to `https://<tenant>.aws.cognee.ai/api/v1/{add,cognify,remember,search,recall}` with an `X-Api-Key` header. The `/api/v1` prefix is required, or you get a 404.

([quickstart](https://docs.cognee.ai/getting-started/quickstart.md), [config](https://docs.cognee.ai/setup-configuration/overview.md), [cloud HTTP](https://docs.cognee.ai/cognee-cloud/http-api.md), [sign-up](https://docs.cognee.ai/cognee-cloud/sign-up.md))

**What they'd likely want built.** I found no fintech examples in their docs and no hackathon-specific offer. The best fit here is an agent that learns from feedback over time: payee and vendor history, past approvals and rejections, and policy documents stored as a graph. The agent queries it before moving money and cites the result in the audit log. That lines up directly with Briefcase's "historical consistency" check and its AI memories. Cognee co-hosted an agentic finance hackathon in Berlin with Dify and N26, so finance is a theme they're interested in ([Berlin event](https://luma.com/ili241vv)).

**Risks and gotchas:**
- **Using Claude as the LLM:** Anthropic works as `LLM_PROVIDER` but not for embeddings. You must also set `EMBEDDING_PROVIDER`, `EMBEDDING_MODEL` and `EMBEDDING_API_KEY` (for example OpenAI or fastembed), or `remember()` fails with `ProviderConfigMismatchError`.
- `remember` runs the full pipeline (chunking, entity extraction, graph build), so it takes a while and costs LLM calls. Pre-load data before the demo and don't do it live.
- Memory can't be recalled until that pipeline finishes.
- The quickstart starts with `forget(everything=True)`, which wipes all data. Remove it once you have data you want to keep.
- Everything is async, and the first run downloads local models.
- With no key set, it falls back to the local `bge-small` embedding model, which is fine for offline testing.

# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

```text
# Briefcase × Stripe Hackathon: London, October 2026

## Overview
- **Format:** An evening hackathon for developers building AI agents that spend and collect money in Stripe test mode. The page's tagline is "Two themes. One night." and promises "three hours to build, two minutes to show it."
- **Date:** Thursday 15 October 2026
- **Schedule:** Doors 17:15; hacking 18:00–21:00
- **Location:** Central London. The address is on the Luma ticket.

## Hosts and Sponsors
- **Briefcase** (Host): AI-native ledger
- **Stripe** (Co-host): Payments infrastructure. Every project moves money through Stripe test mode.
- **Cognee** (Sponsor): Open-source memory platform for agents

## Tracks

### Track 01: Agents that Spend
Build an agent that pays, issues, or moves funds under a policy, and can explain every payment.

**Requirements:**
- Money moves in Stripe test mode, shown in the demo video.
- The agent enforces a written policy covering limits, approvals, and allowed merchants or counterparties.
- The agent answers "why did you pay this?" by citing the rule and the evidence behind it.

**Example ideas:**
- A bill-paying agent that stays within approval limits
- A buying agent with a capped virtual card
- A refunds or disputes agent
- Contractor payouts

**With Cognee:** Store the spending policy and its history in Cognee memory, so the agent can name the clause that authorised each payment and recall why it acted.

### Track 02: Agents that Collect
Build an agent that invoices, meters, or sells without a human raising the bill.

**Requirements:**
- A real-world trigger starts the agent: an email, a contract, usage logs, or a conversation.
- The agent creates a real bill in Stripe test mode, such as an invoice, payment link, checkout session, meter event, or subscription.
- No human raises the bill.

**Example ideas:**
- Usage logs turned into meter events, then an invoice
- An agent that turns a contract into invoices
- A collections agent that remembers each customer's promises and disputes
- An agent that sells to another agent

**With Cognee:** Give sales, billing, and collections agents one shared customer memory.

## Side Quest: Best Use of Cognee Memory
- Open to every team that builds with Cognee, in either track.
- Judged on how central Cognee memory is to the agent's working, and how well the agent explains its actions using that memory.
- Prize announced on the night.

## Prizes
Prizes go to the top three projects across both tracks. The three finalists include a project from each track where possible.

| Place | Prize |
|---|---|
| 1st | £2,000 cash and £5,000 in Stripe credits |
| 2nd | £3,000 in Stripe credits |
| 3rd | £1,000 in Stripe credits |
| Side quest | Best use of Cognee memory (announced on the night) |

## Schedule
- **17:15** Doors open and registration
- **17:45** Briefing: tracks, rules, and judging, then an intro from Cognee
- **18:00** Hacking starts and submissions open
- **19:00** Pizza
- **20:30** Record demo video and submit (editable until 21:00)
- **21:00** Submissions close and judging starts
- **21:25** Three finalists announced
- **21:35** Finalist demos, 3 minutes each
- **21:55** Awards
- **22:00** Close

## Rules
1. Teams of up to 4. Solo entrants are welcome and can find teammates at the briefing.
2. Build during the event. Libraries, starter templates, and APIs are allowed. Commits made before 18:00 are shown to judges.
3. Stripe test mode only. No live keys and no real money.
4. Submit between 18:00 and 21:00 on the submit page with:
   - A public GitHub repo
   - A demo video of 2 minutes or less, hosted on Loom, unlisted YouTube, or a Google Drive link anyone can view
   - Judges stop watching at the 2:00 mark.
5. One submission per team. It can be updated until 21:00.
6. Finalists must be in the room for their 21:35 demo.

## Judging
Six judges split the submissions, and each project is scored out of 100 by one judge. The panel then discusses the leading projects, picks three finalists, and decides 1st, 2nd, and 3rd after the live demos.

| Criterion | Points | What it assesses |
|---|---|---|
| Works end to end | 35 | Money really moves or is billed in Stripe test mode, shown in the demo video |
| Autonomy with control | 25 | The agent acts without a human, within an explicit policy and guardrails |
| Explains every pound | 20 | An audit trail showing why the agent acted |
| Product and creativity | 20 | Whether a finance team would want it, and how original it is |

## Panel
- Ján Stehlík, Briefcase
- Fionn O Colmain, Stripe
- David Gelberg, 10 Downing Street AI team
- Dominic Hudson, AI at Meta
- Akash Bajwa, Earlybird
- Ankit Jain, DeepMind

## Resources for Participants
- **Cognee Cloud credits:** Every participant gets $10 of Cognee Cloud credits. Claim them with the code `cognee35`.
- **Stripe:** Use your own Stripe account in test mode. The page does not offer test accounts or credits beyond the prizes.
- **Briefcase:** The page does not list sandbox, API, or MCP access.

## FAQ Highlights
- **Do I need a team?** No. You can come solo and find teammates at the briefing, or bring up to 4.
- **Can I start before 18:00?** You can plan and read docs, but the project itself must be built from 18:00. Earlier commits are shown to judges.
- **Which Stripe account?** Your own, in test mode.
- **Must I use Cognee?** No. It is optional, but Cognee projects are eligible for the side quest.
- **How do we submit?** Through the submit page, which opens at 18:00 on the day. You need a public GitHub repo and a demo video of 2 minutes or less.
- **What should I bring?** A laptop and a charger. Pizza is provided.

## Links
- Register on Luma: https://luma.com/3k1pazop
- Submit your project: /stripe-october-2026/submit/ (linked at the top of the page; opens at 18:00 on the day)
- Briefcase: https://briefcase.so
- Stripe: https://stripe.com
- Cognee: https://www.cognee.ai/?utm_source=luma&utm_medium=hackathon&utm_campaign=london
```

  RUBRIC (each project scored /100 by ONE judge): Works end to end 35 (money really moves or is billed in Stripe TEST mode, shown in video); Autonomy with control 25 (agent acts without a human, within an explicit written policy and guardrails); Explains every pound 20 (audit trail showing why the agent acted); Product and creativity 20 (would a finance team want it; how original). Three finalists, one from each track where possible. Side quest: Best use of Cognee memory (how central memory is to the agent working, how well the agent explains its actions using memory).
  TRACK 01 "Agents that Spend": pays/issues/moves funds under a WRITTEN policy (limits, approvals, allowed merchants/counterparties) and answers "why did you pay this?" by citing the rule and the evidence. Organiser examples: bill-paying agent within approval limits; buying agent with capped virtual card; refunds/disputes agent; contractor payouts. Cognee suggestion: store policy + history so the agent names the clause that authorised each payment.
  TRACK 02 "Agents that Collect": a real-world trigger (email, contract, usage logs, conversation) starts the agent -> it creates a real bill in Stripe test mode (invoice, payment link, checkout session, meter event, subscription); no human raises the bill. Examples: usage logs -> meter events -> invoice; contract -> invoices; collections agent remembering each customer's promises/disputes; agent sells to another agent. Cognee suggestion: shared customer memory.
  JUDGES: Jan Stehlik (Briefcase CTO & organiser; public thesis "build for verification, not review": agents checked by deterministic rules, every decision explained; their Autopilot gates = re-extraction agrees + data complete + history consistent -> post, else flag; turn-off: a chatbot bolted onto accounting). Fionn O Colmain (Stripe London, organiser; wants real Stripe test-mode flows, idempotency, webhooks; turn-off: mocked payments or an agent with unlimited secret-key power). David Gelberg (10 Downing Street AI team: accountability you can explain in public, readable decision log, human sign-off on exceptions; turn-off: "fully autonomous, no human" with public/consumer money). Dominic Hudson (AI at Meta: sound design and guardrails; turn-off: thin wrapper). Akash Bajwa (Earlybird VC, led Briefcase's seed; writes about agent identity/authorisation as a security category, long-horizon agents, and private evals tied to business outcomes as the moat; wants numbers and a path to a business). Ankit Jain (DeepMind; builds agentic tooling; likes a clean policy/checker separation and automated evals of agent behaviour; turn-off: jumble of agents with no evals/tracing).
  SPONSORS: Briefcase = AI bookkeeping for UK SMEs sold through 200 accounting firms (6,000 businesses); own double-entry Ledger launched 5 Oct 2026; captures receipts via WhatsApp/email, reconciles bank lines, month-end close, VAT/MTD filing; native Stripe feed; supplier payments over open banking gated by approval policies (amount, approver); per-client "AI memories"/contextual learning. Its MCP (50 tools) deliberately CANNOT move money. Cognee = open-source agent memory (knowledge graph + vector), Cognee Cloud HTTP API (add/cognify/remember/search/recall), $10 credits for participants.
  STRIPE SURFACE in the builder's GB test account: CERTAIN = PaymentIntents with test cards, Refunds, Customers, Invoices/InvoiceItems, Payment Links, Checkout, Billing Meters, Subscriptions, Disputes API. LIKELY = Connect transfers to a test connected account; Payouts (test card 4000000000000077 makes balance available immediately). UNKNOWN/RISKY = Issuing virtual cards + real-time authorization webhook (may need enabling in sandbox; 2s timeout), Treasury (UK preview, dashboard setup), Shared Payment Tokens (preview), MPP/402 (sandbox works, stablecoins US-only), agent-tagged restricted keys + approval rules (v2 preview, sandbox unconfirmed).
  STACK (fixed): Next.js + TypeScript single app, Anthropic API (Claude with tool use), Stripe Node SDK, Cognee Cloud via fetch. Web only. Avoid a chat-style UI. Must be demoable at every commit.
  BUILDER'S OWN CANDIDATES (evaluate alongside your own): (A) "Verification, not review" AP agent: supplier invoices in -> deterministic checks (approved vendor, duplicate, budget/limit, supplier bank-detail change = invoice-redirection fraud) -> pays via Stripe transfer -> audit row citing clause + evidence; failures held for one-click human approval; corrections stored in Cognee memory and change future confidence. (B) Cashflow-aware payment scheduler: agent decides WHEN to pay each bill (early-payment discounts vs cash runway floor) within policy, executes, explains savings. (C) Refunds agent under a written refund policy, using customer-history memory, over-limit refunds escalate. (D) Contractor payouts triggered by merged PRs / accepted milestones under a rate-card policy. (E) Contract -> invoices agent (Track 02): extracts billing schedule from a contract, raises Stripe invoices, every line cites the clause + evidence; billing policy caps. (F) Collections agent with memory of promises/disputes, offers payment plans within policy, creates payment links.
  
  
  YOUR LENS: You are a senior Stripe developer advocate in London judging this. Reward projects that use real Stripe test-mode flows correctly and impressively (idempotency keys, metadata, webhooks, dashboard-visible objects) with ZERO setup risk, and penalise anything likely to get stuck on account enablement. Suggest the most impressive-yet-safe money-movement primitives.
  
  Task: propose your top 3 ideas (you may pick, refine or combine the builder's candidates A-F, or propose new ones). For each, fill every field concretely. Score the rubric honestly as the judges would (works /35, autonomy /25, explains /20, product /20). The build_plan must fit ONE person with an AI coding agent in 2h20m and say what is cut.
````text
# Cognee Cloud HTTP API: Extracted Details

The page is an overview. It doesn't document full request schemas or response bodies for most endpoints, so several fields below are marked as not specified.

## Base URL and Auth
- **Base URL:** `https://your-tenant.aws.cognee.ai`. The real host is in the Connection Details card on the API Keys page.
- **Path prefix:** all routes sit under `/api/v1/`. Calling `/api` without the version returns 404.
- **Headers:** `X-Api-Key` carries the key, `X-Tenant-Id` identifies the tenant, and JSON requests set `Content-Type: application/json`.
- Bearer tokens and `/api/v1/auth/login` apply only to self-hosted servers.

## Endpoints

| Endpoint | Method and path | Request body | Response shape |
|---|---|---|---|
| Add | `POST /api/v1/add` | Multipart form. `datasetName` plus repeated `raw_data` for strings, and file uploads. | Not specified |
| Cognify | `POST /api/v1/cognify` | JSON, e.g. `{"datasets": [...]}` | Not specified |
| Remember | `POST /api/v1/remember` | Multipart, like add. Also controls chunking, ontologies, and graph model. | Not specified |
| Search | `POST /api/v1/search` | JSON with `query` (required string) and `search_type`. `datasets` or `dataset_ids` are accepted. | Not specified |
| Recall | `POST /api/v1/recall` | JSON with `query` (required string). Includes session context. | Not specified |
| Datasets | `/api/v1/datasets/*` | Not specified | Not specified. Covers listing, inspecting contents, and deleting a data item or dataset. |
| Quota usage | `GET /api/v1/quotas/usage` | None stated | Not specified |

Other routes mentioned: `POST /api/v1/improve`. Its 409 error body includes an `improve_result` object with a `stages` list.

## Curl Examples (verbatim from the page)

```bash
BASE_URL="https://your-tenant.aws.cognee.ai"

# 1. Add data
curl -X POST "$BASE_URL/api/v1/add" \
  -H "X-Api-Key: $COGNEE_API_KEY" \
  -F "datasetName=my_dataset" \
  -F "raw_data=AI is transforming how we work and live."

# 2. Process it into a knowledge graph
curl -X POST "$BASE_URL/api/v1/cognify" \
  -H "X-Api-Key: $COGNEE_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"datasets": ["my_dataset"]}'

# 3. Search the graph
curl -X POST "$BASE_URL/api/v1/search" \
  -H "X-Api-Key: $COGNEE_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"query": "What is AI?", "search_type": "GRAPH_COMPLETION"}'
```

## Async and Polling
The page doesn't say whether cognify returns a pipeline run ID or how to poll for completion. It only notes that cognify can return a legacy 402 body when the token budget runs out, and that the Activity page shows failed runs.

## Search Types
Only `GRAPH_COMPLETION` appears in the content. The page says to choose a `search_type` to trade depth for latency and points to the Search and Recall page for the rest.

## Errors and Limits
- Errors return `detail` in the form `<message> [<ErrorName>]`, with an optional `remediation` hint.
- Search 500 errors use `{"error", "detail"}`. Recall, remember, and improve 409 errors use `{"error"}`.
- Uploads are capped at 1 GB and 50,000 documents per member. Over-limit adds return 413 and store nothing. Remember is not subject to these limits.

For full schemas, use the OpenAPI docs at `https://api.aws.cognee.ai/docs` or `https://your-tenant.aws.cognee.ai/docs`.
````

```text
**Response shape**

- **Success (POST):** `response_model=list[SearchResult] | list`. The handler returns `jsonable_encoder(results)`, so the body is a JSON list of encoded search results.
- **Errors:** `CogneeApiError` is re-raised for the global handler to convert. Any other exception returns HTTP 500 with an `ErrorResponse` body containing `error` and `detail`.
- **GET history:** returns `list[SearchHistoryItem]`, each with `id`, `text`, `user`, `created_at`, and optional `dataset_id`.
```

```text
I haven't reproduced the full class verbatim. The source-quoting limit caps quoted material at 125 characters, and the page doesn't state a license. You can view the class in the source file directly.

**Payload fields (`RecallPayloadDTO`)**

| Field | Type | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `search_type` | `SearchType \| None` | `None` | Null auto-routes the query; a value pins the strategy. |
| `datasets` | `list[str] \| None` | `None` | Dataset names; null searches all readable datasets. |
| `dataset_ids` | `list[UUID] \| None` | `None` | Takes precedence over `datasets`. |
| `query` | `str` | required | No default. |
| `system_prompt` | `str \| None` | "Answer the question using the provided context. Be as brief as possible." | |
| `node_name` | `list[str] \| None` | `None` | Restricts to node sets. |
| `top_k` | `int \| None` | `15` | |
| `only_context` | `bool` | `False` | Returns the LLM input instead of an answer; no LLM call, nothing written to session. |
| `verbose` | `bool` | `False` | |
| `include_references` | `bool` | `False` | |
| `session_id` | `str \| None` | `None` | Session whose cached QA and trace entries are searched. |
| `scope` | `str \| list[str] \| None` | `None` (treated as `auto`) | Valid values include `graph`, `session`, `session_first`, `trace`, `session_context`, `tools`, `code`, `all`, `auto`. |
| `tool_connections` | `list[str] \| None` | `None` | For the `tools` scope. |
| `stream` | `bool \| None` | `None` | When omitted, the `Accept` header decides. |
| `tools_trigger` | `str` | `"always"` | Or `"on_empty"`. |
| `code_query` | `dict \| None` | `None` | For the `code` scope. |
| `context_profile` | `str` | `"qa"` | Or `"agent"`; used by `session_context`. |
| `response_schema` | `dict \| None` | `None` | JSON Schema for structured output. |

**Response**

- **JSON (default):** a `list[RecallResponse]`, encoded with `jsonable_encoder`.
- **Streaming:** a `StreamingResponse` with `text/event-stream` when `stream` is true, or when `Accept` ranks `text/event-stream` above `application/json`.
- **Errors:**
  - Cognee errors pass through with their own status codes (402/403/404/409/422).
  - An invalid scope name returns 422 with the valid values.
  - Any other exception returns 409 with a generic message.

**Session and context notes**

- With `search_type` omitted and `session_id` set (and no datasets), a session hit can short-circuit the graph search.
- Setting `scope` to `session_first` requests that short-circuit explicitly.
- Pinning `search_type` makes the graph the only source.
- `tools` and `code` run only when explicitly requested, never via `auto` or `all`. `tools` also requires `TOOL_CALLS_ENABLED` on the server.
- The docstring says `include_references` defaults to true, but the field default is `False`. Trust the field default.
```

```typescript
// Thin client for Cognee Cloud (https://docs.cognee.ai/cognee-cloud/http-api).
// All routes live under /api/v1 and authenticate with X-Api-Key.
// If COGNEE_API_KEY is unset every call becomes a no-op that returns null,
// so the app still runs without memory configured.

const BASE = (process.env.COGNEE_BASE_URL ?? "https://api.aws.cognee.ai").replace(/\/$/, "");
const KEY = process.env.COGNEE_API_KEY;

export const cogneeEnabled = Boolean(KEY);

function headers(json = true): Record<string, string> {
  const h: Record<string, string> = { "X-Api-Key": KEY ?? "" };
  if (process.env.COGNEE_TENANT_ID) h["X-Tenant-Id"] = process.env.COGNEE_TENANT_ID;
  if (json) h["Content-Type"] = "application/json";
  return h;
}

async function parse(res: Response) {
  const text = await res.text();
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`cognee ${res.status}: ${text.slice(0, 300)}`);
  try {
    return JSON.parse(text);
  } catch {
    return text;
  }
}

/** Add raw text to a dataset (does not build the graph yet). */
export async function add(dataset: string, texts: string[]) {
  if (!KEY) return null;
  const form = new FormData();
  form.set("datasetName", dataset);
  for (const t of texts) form.append("raw_data", t);
  return parse(await fetch(`${BASE}/api/v1/add`, { method: "POST", headers: headers(false), body: form }));
}

/** Build/refresh the knowledge graph for datasets. Slow (LLM pipeline). */
export async function cognify(datasets: string[]) {
  if (!KEY) return null;
  return parse(
    await fetch(`${BASE}/api/v1/cognify`, { method: "POST", headers: headers(), body: JSON.stringify({ datasets }) }),
  );
}

/** add + cognify in one call. */
export async function remember(dataset: string, texts: string[]) {
  if (!KEY) return null;
  const form = new FormData();
  form.set("datasetName", dataset);
  for (const t of texts) form.append("raw_data", t);
  return parse(await fetch(`${BASE}/api/v1/remember`, { method: "POST", headers: headers(false), body: form }));
}

export type SearchType =
  | "HYBRID_COMPLETION"
  | "GRAPH_COMPLETION"
  | "RAG_COMPLETION"
  | "CHUNKS"
  | "SUMMARIES"
  | "TEMPORAL";

/** Query the graph. Returns the raw list Cognee sends back. */
export async function search(
  query: string,
  opts: { datasets?: string[]; search_type?: SearchType; top_k?: number; only_context?: boolean; system_prompt?: string } = {},
) {
  if (!KEY) return null;
  return parse(
    await fetch(`${BASE}/api/v1/search`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: headers(),
      body: JSON.stringify({ query, search_type: "GRAPH_COMPLETION", top_k: 10, ...opts }),
    }),
  );
}

/** Auto-routed recall across graph + session memory. */
export async function recall(query: string, opts: { datasets?: string[]; top_k?: number; only_context?: boolean } = {}) {
  if (!KEY) return null;
  return parse(
    await fetch(`${BASE}/api/v1/recall`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: headers(),
      body: JSON.stringify({ query, top_k: 10, ...opts }),
    }),
  );
}
```
